reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Rare autosomal recessive deficiency of uroporphyrinogen III synthase, the fourth enzyme of haem biosynthesis, causing one of the most severe cutaneous porphyrias
Typically presents in infancy with pink to red-brown discoloration of the urine staining the nappy and extreme photosensitivity
Severe bullous photodermatosis leads to blistering, scarring, mutilating deformity of the face and digits, and loss of features such as the ears and nose over time
Erythrodontia (red-brown fluorescent teeth) and hypertrichosis are characteristic, and haemolytic anaemia with splenomegaly is common
The block diverts haem synthesis toward non-physiological type I porphyrin isomers, so urine shows greatly raised uroporphyrin I and coproporphyrin I
This is a non-acute, purely photocutaneous porphyria; there are no neurovisceral attacks
Management is largely supportive with rigorous lifelong sunlight avoidance and photoprotection; severe cases may be considered for haematopoietic stem cell transplantation
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria results from markedly deficient uroporphyrinogen III synthase, the fourth enzyme of the haem pathway, which converts hydroxymethylbilane to uroporphyrinogen III. When this step fails, hydroxymethylbilane cyclises non-enzymatically to the type I isomer, which cannot be used for haem and accumulates as uroporphyrin I and coproporphyrin I. These photoreactive type I porphyrins accumulate massively in erythrocytes, plasma, urine, bone and teeth. Deposition in the skin causes light-induced generation of reactive oxygen species and severe phototoxic damage, while porphyrin-laden erythrocytes undergo haemolysis, producing the anaemia and splenomegaly.
additionalDifferentials: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (painful but usually non-blistering photosensitivity)
Xeroderma pigmentosum and other inherited photosensitivity disorders
Hereditary haemolytic anaemias when anaemia dominates
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative urinary porphyrins showing predominant uroporphyrin I and coproporphyrin I
Examination of urine and teeth for characteristic red fluorescence under ultraviolet light (Wood's lamp)
Full blood count and haemolysis screen to detect anaemia and reticulocytosis
Molecular genetic testing of the UROS gene for confirmation and family counselling
Assessment of spleen size and iron status in chronic haemolysis
redFlags: Progressive mutilating scarring with functional loss of digits or facial structures
Secondary infection of ulcerated photodamaged skin
Presentation in a neonate with red-staining urine and blistering requiring urgent photoprotection
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on disease severity; many patients have progressive disfigurement and chronic haemolysis with a substantially affected quality of life, though rigorous photoprotection and, in selected severe cases, stem cell transplantation can improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis in an infant with staining of the nappy dismissed as dietary or infective
Inadequate lifelong photoprotection allowing progressive irreversible damage
Confusing it with erythropoietic protoporphyria, which causes pain without blistering
Underestimating the burden of chronic haemolysis and splenomegaly
Failing to offer genetic counselling given the recessive inheritance
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
